source: The Bhagavadgita, with the Sanatsugatiya and the Anugita (Kashinath Trimbak Telang translation, Sacred Books of the East vol. VIII, 1882)
body: The contacts of the senses, O son of Kunti, which produce cold and heat, pleasure and pain, are not permanent, they are ever coming and going. Bear them, O descendant of Bharata.

_provenance.note: OCR artifacts (stray diacritic marks, ligature breaks) in the archive.org scan corrected by hand against the surrounding sentence; no wording added or paraphrased.

source: The Bhagavadgita, with the Sanatsugatiya and the Anugita (Kashinath Trimbak Telang translation, Sacred Books of the East vol. VIII, 1882)
body: It is not born, nor does it ever die, nor, having existed, does it exist no more. Unborn, everlasting, unchangeable, and primeval, it is not killed when the body is killed.

_provenance.note: OCR artifacts in the archive.org scan corrected by hand against the surrounding sentence; no wording added or paraphrased.

source: The Bhagavadgita, with the Sanatsugatiya and the Anugita (Kashinath Trimbak Telang translation, Sacred Books of the East vol. VIII, 1882)
body: As a man, casting off old clothes, puts on others and new ones, so the embodied self, casting off old bodies, goes to others and new ones.

_provenance.note: Clean OCR; verified verbatim against the scan.

source: The Bhagavadgita, with the Sanatsugatiya and the Anugita (Kashinath Trimbak Telang translation, Sacred Books of the East vol. VIII, 1882)
body: Weapons do not divide it into pieces; fire does not burn it; waters do not moisten it; the wind does not dry it up.

_provenance.note: Clean OCR; verified verbatim against the scan.

source: The Bhagavadgita, with the Sanatsugatiya and the Anugita (Kashinath Trimbak Telang translation, Sacred Books of the East vol. VIII, 1882)
body: For to one that is born, death is certain; and to one that dies, birth is certain.

_provenance.note: Clean OCR; verified verbatim against the scan.

source: The Bhagavadgita, with the Sanatsugatiya and the Anugita (Kashinath Trimbak Telang translation, Sacred Books of the East vol. VIII, 1882)
body: Your business is with action alone; not by any means with fruit. Let not the fruit of action be your motive to action. Let not your attachment be fixed on inaction.

_provenance.note: A proper name in this verse (Dhananjaya, an epithet of Arjuna) was garbled by OCR and omitted rather than guessed; the quoted sentences are otherwise verbatim and unaffected by the omission.

source: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man (Charles Johnston translation, 1912)
body: Union, spiritual consciousness, is gained through control of the versatile psychic nature.

source: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man (Charles Johnston translation, 1912)
body: Then the Seer comes to consciousness in his proper nature.

source: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man (Charles Johnston translation, 1912)
body: The right use of the will is the steady effort to stand in spiritual being.

source: The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali: The Book of the Spiritual Man (Charles Johnston translation, 1912)

source: The Vishnu Purana: A System of Hindu Mythology and Tradition (Horace Hayman Wilson translation, 1840; this scan of the 1864 edition)
body: Every man reaps the consequences of his own acts. Anger is the destruction of all that man obtains, by arduous exertions, of fame and of devout austerities, and prevents the attainment of heaven or of emancipation. Mercy is the might of the righteous.

_provenance.note: This scan is heavily interleaved with Wilson's own footnotes and untranscribed Devanagari, both skipped; the quoted sentences are drawn only from the clean narrative body (Parasara's speech to Maitreya) and cross-checked word-for-word against the scan. Most of this edition was NOT usable for verbatim quotation without guessing at OCR-garbled words, so only this one passage was pulled from it -- flagging that a better scan of this translation would be needed to draw more from it responsibly.

source: The Markandeya Purana (Frederick Eden Pargiter translation, Bibliotheca Indica, Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1904)
body: As Vishnu is chief among the gods, as the brahman chief among men, and as the crest-jewel chief among all decorations, as the axe is the best among weapons, as the mind best among the organs, so in this world is the Mahabharata the best among all the Sastras.

_provenance.note: OCR rendered 'brahman' as 'hrahman'; corrected by hand as an unambiguous single-letter scan error, no other change made.

source: The Markandeya Purana (Frederick Eden Pargiter translation, Bibliotheca Indica, Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1904)
body: Here are described both Wealth and Virtue, Love, and Final emancipation from transmigration. It is the best Dharma-sastra, it is the most eminent Artha-sastra; it too is the foremost Kama-sastra, as well as the noblest Moksha-sastra.

source: The Markandeya Purana (Frederick Eden Pargiter translation, Bibliotheca Indica, Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1904)
body: Just as one sunk in water, on emerging from it, seems to be born from water and flings the water away, so Brahma is both Prakriti and the Soul.

_provenance.note: OCR artifacts ('w^ater' -> 'water', 'Bi*ahma' -> 'Brahma', 'horn' -> 'born') corrected by hand against the surrounding sentence; canto/verse numbering approximate, taken from the nearest printed verse markers in this scan rather than a critical edition.
